questions.q: What was the "non-Congressism" strategy articulated by Ram Manohar Lohia, and which two types of electoral arrangements did opposition parties adopt under it?
questions.a: Non-Congressism was Lohia's argument that Congress rule was undemocratic and anti-poor, so ideologically disparate opposition parties should unite to reclaim democracy. They formed anti-Congress fronts (pre-poll alliances) in some states and entered seat-sharing adjustments in others. A wrong answer (e.g., "non-Congressism meant merging all parties into one") reveals confusion between electoral alliances and party mergers — Lohia explicitly opposed merger, favouring tactical unity.

questions.q: Why did the Congress lose majority in seven states in 1967 despite winning a Lok Sabha majority? Explain using the concepts of "performance legitimacy" and "split-vote effect."
questions.a: The Congress lost state majorities because economic distress (drought, price rise, devaluation) eroded its performance legitimacy at the state level where voters blamed local Congress governments, while the opposition's non-Congress fronts consolidated anti-Congress votes (avoiding split-vote effect). At the national level, Congress retained a Lok Sabha majority because the opposition unity was less complete and Indira Gandhi's leadership still commanded residual loyalty. A wrong answer attributing state losses solely to "Indira's inexperience" misses the structural role of opposition coordination and state-level anti-incumbency.

questions.q: In the 1967 elections, the Congress won 283 Lok Sabha seats (out of 520) with 40.8% vote share — its lowest since 1952. If the opposition had formed a unified national front instead of state-level alliances, apply the FPTP mechanics to explain how the seat outcome might have differed.
questions.a: Under FPTP, a unified national opposition front would have concentrated the anti-Congress vote (approx. 59%) in each constituency, likely converting many Congress pluralities into opposition majorities — potentially denying Congress a Lok Sabha majority. The actual state-level alliances left anti-Congress votes divided in many seats, letting Congress win with ~41%. A wrong answer claiming "vote share directly determines seats" ignores FPTP's disproportionality: Congress won 54% seats with 41% votes because opposition votes were fragmented.

questions.q: Compare the SVD (Samyukt Vidhayak Dal) governments in Bihar and Punjab after 1967. What does their ideological composition reveal about the nature of non-Congressism as a governing strategy?
questions.a: Bihar's SVD included socialists (SSP, PSP), CPI (left), and Jana Sangh (right); Punjab's Popular United Front included rival Akali factions, both communist parties, SSP, Republican Party, and Jana Sangh. This ideological incoherence — left and right governing together — reveals non-Congressism was a negative coalition (anti-Congress) without a positive programme, making SVDs unstable. A wrong answer calling them "ideological alliances" misses Lohia's explicit framing: unity only for "reclaiming democracy," not policy consensus.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The 'Aya Ram, Gaya Ram' phenomenon after 1967 was a symptom of weak party institutionalisation, not just individual opportunism." Use the Haryana case of Gaya Lal to support your judgment.
questions.a: The statement is correct. Gaya Lal changed parties thrice in a fortnight (Congress → United Front → Congress → United Front in 9 hours), and Congress leader Rao Birendra Singh publicly celebrated his return ("Gaya Ram was now Aya Ram"). This shows party structures enabled defections — leaders actively recruited defectors to form governments, and no anti-defection law existed. A wrong answer blaming only "greedy MLAs" ignores that party bosses (like Rao Birendra Singh) incentivised floor-crossing, reflecting systemic weakness in party discipline and organisational loyalty.

questions.q: Draft a one-paragraph argument (4-5 sentences) that a Congress Syndicate leader might have written in 1967 defending the party's continued dominance, and a counter-argument from a non-Congressism supporter. Both must use evidence from the 1967 verdict.
questions.a: Syndicate defence: "Congress remains the only national party with a Lok Sabha majority (283 seats) and governance experience; state losses reflect local anti-incumbency, not national rejection — voters still trust Congress at the Centre." Non-Congressism counter: "Congress lost 7 states, half its cabinet ministers, and tallest organisers (Kamaraj, Patil); its vote share plummeted to 40.8% — the 'Congress System' of accommodation has collapsed, and only united opposition can prevent authoritarian drift." A poor answer uses generic slogans without citing specific 1967 data (seat tally, vote share, ministerial defeats, state losses).
